title: Sulfur speciation shapes rhizosphere responses of Zostera marina, with thiosulfate as a key intermediate
content:
Abstract

Sulfur cycling is a dominant biogeochemical process in coastal zone sediments yet the role of sulfur speciation in coordinating plant and microbial responses remains poorly revealed. Using integrated plant physiology, metabolomics, transcriptomics, and microbial functional gene analyses, we show that distinct sulfur forms (sulfide, thiosulfate, sulfate, and thiourea) differentially restructure the Zostera marina rhizosphere system. The low concentration (1 mM) of the intermediate-valence sulfur species thiosulfate elicited the strongest growth-promoting physiological responses. Functional gene analysis revealed sulfur-form-specific shifts in rhizosphere sulfur-cycling potential, including increased abundances of sqr and DsrB and a decrease in soxB under thiosulfate exposure. Moderate thiosulfate concentrations (2 mM) induced widespread metabolic activation in Z. marina, whereas higher concentrations (4 mM) led to a transition toward a strategy centered on growth maintenance and basal metabolism at both the transcriptional and metabolic levels. A Roseobacter clade strain Sulfitobacter alexandrii was applied to investigate how thiosulfate availability affects plant-microbe interactions. This study provides a conceptual framework for understanding sulfur-driven coupling processes in seagrass ecosystems.
